profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the Data Science workstream and the Credit Product workstream at a supply chain finance provider preparing a 6-week pilot of an invoice dilution prediction service. The company has built a two-stage leakage-free modeling pipeline using XGBoost, KAN, and an ensemble layer, and now needs to align on handoffs between model scoring, dashboard delivery, and risk operations review for a pilot focused on dynamic credit limits for mid-market buyers without mandatory IPUs. The agenda is to confirm which data extract will feed the pilot, what 'pilot-ready' means for each team, how coverage for buyer-supplier pairs will be handled in the first release, and who owns the backtest and monitoring artifacts. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on next steps, file handoffs, and timeline for pilot launch.

members.name: Asha Menon
members.expertise: Machine learning for credit and non-credit risk, feature engineering, temporal validation, model deployment handoffs
members.background: Asha joined from a fintech lender and has spent the last year building the dilution prediction framework across invoice, dispute, and payment behavior data; she works closely with data engineering but is not embedded with front-line risk operations.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to launch with technically clean inputs and a defensible offline evaluation package, and she is worried that operational teams will push for broader deployment conditions that introduce leakage, sparse-history misuse, or avoidable support work before the model is stabilized.
hidden_assumptions: When someone asks for the 'approved extract,' they mean the curated feature snapshot after finance-ops reversals and duplicate corrections have been applied, not the raw nightly warehouse table.

A 'pilot-ready' model in a coordination setting means scores, documentation, and validation outputs are ready for shadow use by a small risk team, even if no production-facing dashboard automation is complete yet.

Coverage for buyer-supplier pairs naturally refers to pairs that meet the model's minimum history threshold, while thin-file or brand-new pairs stay on the deterministic rules engine outside the model scope.

A 'leakage-free backtest file' is a frozen evaluation artifact keyed to invoice approval date and should not be casually refreshed with later quarters without re-running the full temporal split logic.

members.name: Daniel Reeves
members.role: Senior Product Manager, Trade Finance Risk Platforms
members.expertise: Cross-functional rollout of risk tools, dashboard workflows, pilot execution, credit operations enablement
members.background: Daniel came from a large bank's trade finance transformation team and now coordinates between credit policy, operations, and data teams to operationalize scoring tools inside existing underwriting and limit-management workflows.
members.private_state: He wants a visible pilot that risk managers can use in their normal workflow, and he is concerned about stakeholder confidence if the first release excludes too many counterparties or depends on bespoke analyst interpretation.
hidden_assumptions: The 'approved extract' is the official nightly warehouse snapshot already recognized by operations and BI, because anything else creates reconciliation questions during pilot review.
If something is 'pilot-ready,' it should appear in the risk dashboard with a daily refresh, basic exception handling, and enough stability that users do not need to interpret ad hoc files.
Coverage for buyer-supplier pairs includes all currently onboarded pairs in the selected pilot book, even if some receive fallback outputs rather than pure model scores.

A shared folder labeled 'leakage_free' is an operationally safe working asset that can be extended with the latest quarter for business review, unless someone explicitly says it is frozen for research only.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using the 'approved extract' for the pilot feed.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the curated modeling snapshot produced after finance-ops adjustments, duplicate removals, and post-booking corrections are applied in the feature store.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the official nightly warehouse extract already used by operations reporting and dashboard reconciliation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both versions are legitimately 'approved' inside their own workstreams, and because the meeting is about coordination rather than data design, the phrase sounds settled and routine rather than something needing unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the model should be 'pilot-ready by the end of the month.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the model package, score file, validation summary, and usage notes are complete enough for a controlled shadow review with a few risk analysts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the scores are integrated into the underwriting dashboard with a daily refresh and minimal workflow support so credit managers can use them in normal limit discussions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'pilot-ready' is common shorthand in business meetings, and both parties assume the other shares the same operational maturity threshold because they both support launching a pilot on the same date.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need coverage for the pilot buyer-supplier pairs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means model coverage for pairs with sufficient historical observations to support the two-stage model, excluding thin-file and newly onboarded pairs from the ML output.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means every currently onboarded pair in the selected pilot population should receive some pilot-era output, whether from the model or an implicit fallback, because the risk team will expect a complete view.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They both use the same word 'coverage' while focusing on different boundaries—technical eligibility versus operational population—and the existence of a deterministic baseline makes each interpretation feel naturally compatible.

misalignment_points.topic: How to handle the 'leakage-free backtest file'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to reusing the 'leakage-free backtest file' for pilot review materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the file is a frozen research artifact built with strict temporal splits by invoice approval date, and any update requires rerunning the whole validation pipeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the existing shared file can simply be appended with the latest quarter's results for stakeholder review, since the folder already marks it as leakage-free.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the goal of using a validated historical file, but the operational method for maintaining that file differs silently; in a status-oriented meeting, neither side is likely to pause over whether 'reuse' means freeze or extend.

I also want to keep coverage scoped to buyer-supplier pairs that actually meet the minimum history threshold; thin-file pairs should stay on deterministic rules until we know the support burden.
